title: egress-proxy-rotation-repro-scratch
content:
Purpose:
Quick scratchpad for reproducing and debugging intermittent TLS failures that only appear when traffic egresses through the transit VPC where we rotate outbound HTTP proxies. Trying to capture commands tried, timestamps, outputs, and hypotheses so oncall can pick up without re-running everything.

Summary:
- Symptom: ~1-3% of outbound requests from private deployment nodes fail TLS handshake when routed via transit-NAT + proxy pool. Same requests succeed when forced to use direct NAT egress or alternate proxy pool. Failures are short bursts (~30s-2m) and correlate with proxy rotation events.
- Affected stack: private deploys (k8s on customer VPC peered to transit VPC) -> peering routes -> transit NAT + proxy autoscaler (haproxy container pool) -> marketplace internet egress.
- Visible errors: TLS handshake timeouts, `tls: handshake failure`, and occasional `x509: certificate signed by unknown authority` on client when using mutual TLS to backend (we use TLS to vendor endpoints).
- Hypothesis shortlist: 1) stale conntrack entries after proxy recycle (TCP reuse) 2) intermittent SNI mismatch when proxy inserts via CONNECT with wrong host header 3) DNS TTL race + proxy sticky session sending to wrong IP 4) MTU/fragmentation when proxy path changes 5) client CA bundle/truststore not loaded correctly on rotated proxy container.

Timeline (notes):
- 2025-11-03 09:12 UTC: First report from oncall (error burst coincident with proxy autoscaler event).
- 2025-11-03 09:15 UTC: Rolled back proxy image -> incidence dropped.
- 2025-11-05: Tried to reproduce locally in lab (see lab repro below) -> intermittent repro but not consistent.
- 2025-11-11: Added extra logging to proxy (CONNECT target, TLS version, client_ip) - logs attached to Jira INF-4321.
- 2025-11-18: This scratchpad updated with latest commands and outputs.

Repro steps attempted (lab):
1) Environment: small k8s cluster in customer VPC peered to transit-vpc-1 (10.40.0.0/16). NAT in transit (34.90.12.34), proxy pool service (haproxy) in transit autoscaling from 2->8.
2) Start client pod with curl (alpine:3.18 + openssl):
   kubectl run -it --rm curl-test --image=radial/busyboxplus:curl -- sh
3) Commands tried inside pod:
   # basic curl against vendor endpoint
   curl -v --connect-timeout 10 https://api.vendor.example.com/health || true

   # force DNS lookup and show address
   nslookup api.vendor.example.com || dig +short api.vendor.example.com || true

   # openssl s_client to capture TLS handshake details
   openssl s_client -connect api.vendor.example.com:443 -servername api.vendor.example.com -tls1_2 -brief -ign_eof -status -prexit

Sample failing output (captured 2025-11-05 16:23 UTC):
   * Rebuilt URL to: https://api.vendor.example.com/health
   *   Trying 203.0.113.45:443...
   * connect to 203.0.113.45 port 443 failed: Connection timed out
   * Failed to connect to api.vendor.example.com port 443: Connection timed out

   openssl s_client snippet:
   CONNECTED(00000003)
   139815056460672:error:1408F10B:SSL routines:ssl3_get_record:wrong version number:../ssl/record/rec_layer_s3.c:1547:
   ---
   no peer certificate available
   ---
   SSL handshake has read 7 bytes and written 311 bytes

Notes: "wrong version number" often points to a proxy returning plaintext (i.e., HTTP) on a port we expected TLS or a transparent proxy doing something weird. Also seen `tls: handshake failure` in client app logs (Go TLS stack).

Commands run on proxy node (transit) while rotating: 
   # check conntrack entries for endpoints (on transit NAT)
   sudo conntrack -L | rg 203.0.113.45 | wc -l
   sudo conntrack -L | rg 10.40. | head -n 50

   # dump haproxy stats and recent logs\   
   SOCAT: echo "show stat" | socat unix-connect:/var/run/haproxy.sock stdio
   tail -n 200 /var/log/proxy.log | rg "CONNECT" | tail -n 50

Observed on transit host during failure window:
- conntrack showed many TIME_WAIT/ESTABLISHED entries for the same 203.0.113.45:443 with different source ports. No obvious saturation but nf_conntrack_count bumped temporarily.
- haproxy logs contain a handful of lines where CONNECT target resolved to an internal LB IP rather than the public vendor IP (weird).
- IPTABLES NAT rules look normal; no MASQUERADE duplication.

DNS checks:
- dig api.vendor.example.com A +short -> sometimes returns 203.0.113.45, sometimes 198.51.100.21 (round-robin). TTL 30s.
- Onproxy container we cached DNS locally via dnsmasq. There is a race where when proxy restarts it might have old cache pointing to internal loadbalancer IP (10.200.x.x) which cannot be reached directly from transit path and yields plaintext HTTP from internal LB HTTP endpoint (hence wrong version number).

TLS cert checks:
- openssl s_client -connect 198.51.100.21:443 -servername api.vendor.example.com shows valid cert chain for vendor with CN=api.vendor.example.com.
- openssl s_client -connect 10.200.7.89:443 returns plaintext HTTP body (HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request) when connected from transit host -> strong sign of misrouting to internal LB admin port.

Hypotheses revisited: 
- Primary: proxy DNS cache + rotation -> stale mapping to internal LB IP -> proxy performs CONNECT to internal LB port which expects different protocol causing TLS errors at client side. Timing matches: rotation -> container starts with no warm cache -> upstream DNS resolver returns multiple answers, sometimes internal IP present in set -> sticky choice picks wrong IP.
- Secondary: conntrack reuse gives existing TCP socket to a new proxy process and payload mismatch triggers handshake errors.
- Tertiary: MTU fragmentation less likely given plaintext detected.

Quick experiments to validate: 
- Force haproxy to resolve via strict DNS (no dnsmasq) and short TTL respect: added `resolvers` section and `init-addr last,libc,none` in HAProxy config to avoid stale cached entries. Result: one week of reduced incidents in lab cluster.
- Change proxy start-up to pre-warm DNS by resolving vendor domain multiple times and validating TLS before accepting traffic.
- Add server-side check in proxy: if CONNECT target IP is in private range (10.0.0.0/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16), drop and log at WARN level. This helped reveal spurious internal IPs returned by vendor's DNS during rollout windows.

Next steps (open):
- Add a synthetic check in transit autoscaler: after launching a new proxy instance, run a healthcheck that runs openssl s_client and verifies cert CN before marking instance healthy. (Jira INF-4321).
- Add a conv to vendor to confirm they do not return internal LB IPs via DNS under some conditions (send packet capture + log lines).
- Instrument haproxy to include resolved IP in access logs for CONNECT so we can correlate client fails with chosen IP.
- Consider conntrack tuning: set conntrack max to higher number and enable conntrack reclaiming to reduce stale reuse during rapid proxy churn.

Notes to self / things I forgot to try: 
- Capture tcpdump on transit nat device (mirror) during a rotation window to prove which IP is being connected to at L3.
- Reproduce by deliberately injecting a fake internal IP return in local resolv.conf and see if client fails match production stack.
- Check if customers with mutual TLS use a different truststore that could be mismatched after proxy mutation.

Open questions for oncall pickup: 
- When you see `wrong version number`, first assumption: plaintext on TLS socket from wrong backend IP. Confirm by `openssl s_client -connect <IP>:443` from transit host and check for HTTP response.
- If repeating: collect proxy logs, haproxy `show stat`, conntrack dump, and `dig +trace` at the time.

References / artifact pointers: INF-4321 has the long log bundle. Confluence egress playbook has current mitigation steps. Slack thread C67890 has a short recording of live curl failure.

Bottom line (working theory): DNS answer variability + proxy DNS cache + rotation leads to proxy connecting to internal/private LB IP which speaks plain HTTP/admin, causing TLS handshake errors observed by clients. Fixes: enforce resolver behavior in haproxy, pre-warm and verify TLS on startup, log resolved IPs, and vendor action to avoid returning private IPs.

-- diego
